tip: ‘Paling lambat’ is literally 'at the slowest' and means 'at the latest': ‘konfirmasi paling lambat hari Jumat’ – the deadline phrase of letters and forms.
‘Kesalahan penulisan’ = 'clerical error', letter-speak – spoken: ‘ada salah ketik’ (there's a typo).
‘Riwayat hidup’ = 'curriculum vitae' – job-application word; in speech people just say ‘CV’.
‘Demikian surat ini kami buat’ = 'thus we have written this letter' – the classic closing line of official letters.
‘Di tempat’ on an envelope = 'at your address' – used when the writer skips the full address.
‘Bahwa’ = 'that' introducing a clause – written style; conversation usually drops it.
‘Hadir’ is the formal version of ‘datang’ (come) – meeting language; spoken: ‘datang ya, jangan telat’ (come, don't be late).
‘Berdasarkan’ = 'based on' – report language; in speech: ‘dari hasil rapat’ (from the meeting results).
‘Bergerak di bidang’ = 'operates in the field of' – company-profile wording, rarely heard in speech.
‘Belum dapat kami penuhi’ is the polite refusal of letters; spoken: ‘maaf, belum bisa’ (sorry, can't yet).
‘Pihak’ = 'party, side' (‘pihak perusahaan’ = the company) – contract wording, not everyday speech.
‘Apabila’ = formal 'if' – letters and rules; conversation nearly always uses ‘kalau’.
‘Sebagaimana mestinya’ = 'as it should be' – the boilerplate that closes official certificates.
On signs, ‘dilarang’ = 'it is prohibited' – spoken: ‘tidak boleh merokok di sini’.
‘Dengan tertib’ = 'in an orderly way' – sign wording; spoken: ‘antre yang rapi ya’.
‘Ketidaknyamanannya’ = 'the inconvenience': ‘ketidaknyamanan’ (built from ‘tidak nyaman’, not comfortable) plus ‘-nya’ (the).
‘Pelanggar’ = 'violator', from ‘melanggar’ (to break a rule) – sign and law vocabulary.
The ending ‘-lah’ makes a polite written command: forms say ‘isilah’ (fill in), people say ‘tolong diisi’.
‘Pemohon’ = 'the applicant', from ‘memohon’ (to request) – form vocabulary; spoken: ‘yang mengajukan’.
Commands drop the ‘me-’ prefix: forms say ‘lampirkan’ (attach), not ‘melampirkan’. A ‘me-...-kan’ verb loses ‘me-’ when it becomes an instruction.
‘Dilarang’ + verb is the sign formula for 'No ...-ing': ‘dilarang berjualan’ = no selling. Swap in another verb and you can read most street signs.
‘Sedang berlangsung’ = 'is in progress' – notice-board phrase; spoken: ‘lagi ada ujian’.
Signs speak formally: ‘pengunjung dilarang membawa makanan’. Said aloud, the same rule is just ‘tidak boleh bawa makanan’ – the formal noun dropped, ‘membawa’ clipped to ‘bawa’.
Sign word: ‘pemegang kartu’ = 'card holder', from ‘pegang’ (to hold); spoken: ‘yang punya kartu anggota’.
‘Alas kaki’ = 'footwear', the sign word – in speech people just say ‘sepatu dan sandal’ (shoes and sandals).
‘Kawasan’ = official 'zone, area' – sign vocabulary; in conversation people say ‘daerah’.
‘Yang tersedia’ = 'that are provided, available' – notice phrasing; spoken: ‘yang ada’.
‘Telepon genggam’ = official 'mobile phone' – in real life nearly everyone says ‘HP’ (pronounced ha-pe).
‘Keadaan darurat’ = 'an emergency situation' – ‘keadaan’ (state, condition) makes phrases sound official.
‘Wajib’ = 'must (by rule)' – sign word; spoken: ‘harus pakai masker’.
